Chambers of the Priests: Measurements of the Temple.</title> <div sID="gen21430" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11849"/><hi type="bold">2. Before the length of an hundred cubits--</hi>that is, before "the separate place," which was that length (<reference osisRef="Ezek.41.13">Eze 41:13</reference>). He had before spoken of chambers for the officiating priests on the north and south gates of the inner court (<reference osisRef="Ezek.40.44-Ezek.40.46">Eze 40:44-46</reference>). He now returns to take a more exact view of them. <div eID="gen21430" type="x-p"/>

entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11850"/><div sID="gen21431" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11850"/><hi type="bold">5. shorter--</hi>that is, the building became narrower as it rose in height. The chambers were many: so "in My Father's house are many mansions" (<reference osisRef="John.14.2">Joh 14:2</reference>); and besides these there was much "room" still left (compare <reference osisRef="Luke.14.22">Lu 14:22</reference>). The chambers, though private, were near the temple. Prayer in our chambers is to prepare us for public devotions, and to help us in improving them. <div eID="gen21431" type="x-p"/>

entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11851"/><div sID="gen21432" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11851"/><hi type="bold">16. five hundred reeds--</hi>the Septuagint substitutes "cubits" for "reeds," to escape the immense compass assigned to the whole, namely, a square of five hundred rods or three thousand cubits (two feet each; <reference osisRef="Ezek.40.5">Eze 40:5</reference>), in all a square of one and one-seventh miles, that is, more than all ancient Jerusalem; also, there is much space thus left unappropriated. Fairbairn rightly supports English Version, which agrees with the Hebrew. The vast extent is another feature marking the ideal character of the temple. It symbolizes the great enlargement of the kingdom of God, when Jehovah-Messiah shall reign at Jerusalem, and from thence to the ends of the earth (<reference osisRef="Isa.2.2-Isa.2.4">Is 2:2-4</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.3.17">Jr 3:17</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rom.11.12">Ro 11:12</reference>, <reference osisRef="Rom.11.15">15</reference>). <div eID="gen21432" type="x-p"/>

It symbolizes the great enlargement of the kingdom of God, when Jehovah-Messiah shall reign at Jerusalem, and from thence to the ends of the earth ( Is 2:2-4 ; Jr 3:17 ; Ro 11:12 , 15 ).

entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11852"/><div sID="gen21433" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11852"/><hi type="bold">20. wall ... separation between ... sanctuary and ... profane--</hi>No longer shall the wall of partition be to separate the Jew and the Gentile (<reference osisRef="Eph.2.14">Ep 2:14</reference>), but to separate the sacred from the profane. The lowness of it renders it unfit for the purpose of defense (the object of the wall, <reference osisRef="Rev.21.12">Re 21:12</reference>). But its square form (as in the city, <reference osisRef="Rev.21.16">Re 21:16</reference>) is the emblem of the kingdom that cannot be shaken (<reference osisRef="Heb.12.28">He 12:28</reference>), resting on prophets and apostles, Jesus Christ being the chief corner-stone. <chapter eID="Ezek.42"/>
